lead: The “Valencian Sistine Chapel”. Almost 2,000 m² of Baroque frescoes designed by Palomino cover a 15th-century Gothic structure in the most surprising monument in Valencia’s historic centre.

The Church of San Nicolás de Bari and San Pedro Mártir — popularly known as San Nicolás — is the monument that most surprises visitors to Valencia who walk in without knowing what awaits them. The outer façade is discreet, typical of a medieval Gothic church in El Carmen district. The interior is a visual spectacle without precedent in the city.

The title “Valencian Sistine Chapel” is no tourist metaphor: it was suggested in 2012 by the very director of the restoration of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican, Gianluigi Colalucci, after visiting the church. The full restoration, financed entirely by the Fundación Hortensia Herrero, restored the 17th-century frescoes to all their original splendour in 2019.

items.kicker: The heart of the monument · ~2,000 m² of fresco painting
items.title: The Vault · The Frescoes of Palomino and Dionís Vidal
items.subtitle: Antonio Palomino (design) · Dionís Vidal (execution) · 1690–1693
items.body: The vault of San Nicolás is the closest thing to the Sistine Chapel you will find in Spain. Almost 2,000 square metres of fresco paintings completely cover the vaults, ribs and columns of the church, narrating the most important episodes in the lives of the patron saints: Saint Nicholas the Bishop and Saint Peter Martyr. The iconographic programme was designed by Antonio Palomino — court painter to King Charles II, called to Valencia in 1697 — and executed by the Valencian artist Dionís Vidal. The nickname “Valencian Sistine Chapel” was suggested in 2012 by the very director of the restoration of the Sistine Chapel in Rome, Gianluigi Colalucci, after visiting San Nicolás.
facts: Almost 2,000 m² of fresco paintings · Vaults, ribs, apses and columns

items.kicker: 13th–17th century · Two styles in perfect coexistence
items.title: The Architecture · Gothic Covered in Baroque
items.subtitle: Valencian Gothic 15th c. · Baroque transformation 1690–1693 · Juan Bta. Pérez Castiel
items.body: The Church of San Nicolás de Bari and San Pedro Mártir is the best example in Valencia — and probably in Spain — of a Gothic structure coexisting with Baroque decoration in a single space. The original church was founded by James I in the 13th century after the Christian conquest, donated to the Dominicans on the site of a mosque. In the 15th century it reached its present dimensions: a single nave of six bays with side chapels between the buttresses and a polygonal presbytery. Between 1690 and 1693, the architect Juan Bautista Pérez Castiel — also master builder of the Central Market and Valencia Cathedral — transformed the Baroque interior: he softened the arches and vaults with stucco, preparing the surface for Palomino’s frescoes.
facts: Gothic, 15th c. · One nave, 6 bays, side chapels, polygonal presbytery
1690–1693 · Juan Bautista Pérez Castiel · Stucco on arches and vaults

items.kicker: Pioneering digital experience · Included in the ticket
items.title: “The Light of San Nicolás” · Immersive experience
items.subtitle: Video mapping on the vault · Interactive room · Multimedia room · Every hour
items.body: The Light of San Nicolás is a permanent immersive project that fuses history, art and advanced technology in three artistic interventions. The projection “Homage to Beauty” — with video mapping on the vault, light and 21st-century music — runs on the hour every hour from 11:00 and brings Palomino’s Baroque frescoes to life. The interactive room “The Heartbeat of San Nicolás” combines chronological totems with animations and music. The multimedia room “Lux ex Oriente” evokes the saint’s attributes through a stained-glass window of light. It is one of the most advanced digital heritage experiences in Spain.

items.title: The Restoration · Patronage of the 21st Century
items.subtitle: Innovative techniques · Microbacteria · Projection lighting
items.body: The recovery of San Nicolás has been made possible thanks to the full patronage of the Fundación Hortensia Herrero, with an investment of 4.7 million euros between 2012 and 2021. The restoration used pioneering techniques never before used in Spain: cleaning of the frescoes using non-pathogenic microbacteria bred in the laboratory, which remove the encrusted dirt without affecting the paint. The process was completed in several phases: main nave (2012–2019), Communion Chapel (2017–2018) and Baroque Sacristy and Trasagrario (2021). The frescoes look today as they did at the end of the 17th century, when Dionís Vidal completed his exceptional pictorial cycle.
facts: Fundación Hortensia Herrero · Fully funded · 4.7 million euros

items.kicker: Valencian painting of the Golden Age · Chapter House
items.title: The Collection · Masterpieces in the Chapels
items.subtitle: Joan de Joanes · Jerónimo Jacinto de Espinosa · Orrente · Esteban March
items.body: Beyond the vault frescoes, San Nicolás treasures an extraordinary collection of sacred art. The Chapter House — an irregularly shaped space with a ribbed vault that practically preserves its original 15th-century appearance — brings together major works by Valencian painters of the Golden Age: Juan de Joanes, Jerónimo Jacinto de Espinosa, Pedro de Orrente and Esteban March. The Chapel of the Crucifixion stands out, with its altarpiece formed by an image of Christ Crucified against a painted background by Vicente Macip and his son Joan de Joanes. The Baroque organ at the high altar completes the extraordinary heritage ensemble.
facts: 15th century · Original ribbed vault · Juanes, Espinosa, Orrente, March

items.kicker: Religious tradition · Every Monday of the year
items.title: The Mondays of San Nicolás · Living Devotion
items.subtitle: Hundreds of the faithful · Protector of children and the family · Weekly pilgrimage
items.body: Every Monday of the year, hundreds of the faithful come to the Parish of San Nicolás to ask for the intercession of the saint, protector of children, of the family and of sailors. The “Mondays of San Nicolás” are among the most deeply rooted religious traditions in Valencia, making this small church in El Carmen district one of the most popular places of devotion in the city. San Nicolás remains a living parish that combines its role as a cultural monument with active liturgical life: on Mondays the church is closed to tourism, open only for worship. The saint’s feast day is celebrated on 6 December.
facts: Weekly pilgrimage of the faithful · Church closed to tourism · Worship only

blocks.title: Tips for visiting San Nicolás
items: The “Light of San Nicolás” video mapping is projected every hour from 11:00 — arrive 10 min early for the best spot
Be ready to look up: the vault is the show, not the side walls
The audio guide in 5 languages is included in the ticket: use it to understand each lunette of the vault (45 min tour)
On Mondays it is closed to tourism: if you want to see the “Mondays of San Nicolás”, access is as a worshipper only
The church is a 5 min walk from the Cathedral along Calle Caballeros — combine both visits in the same morning
The combined ticket with the Hortensia Herrero Art Centre (€22) is the best option if you visit both monuments
